abstract: This paper offers a practical guide and case study for integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into content analysis as a way to augment or replace human coders. The authors demonstrate their approach by replicating and extending Feldman et al.'s (2015) study of U.S. newspaper coverage of climate change, running a locally hosted Llama 3.1-70b model on consumer-grade hardware. They validate LLM coding against original human codes, scale the analysis tenfold, and extend it to a comparable German-language corpus, providing a replicable agentic workflow and guidelines for prompting, validation, and multilingual coding.
key_claims: LLMs can replicate human content-analysis coding at acceptable reliability while running locally on consumer-grade hardware, addressing cost, scalability, and data-privacy constraints.
A structured agentic workflow combining an Instructor, Classifier, Judge, and Human Intermediary improves coding accuracy, consistency, and transparency over single-pass approaches.
LLMs enable richer, more granular coding (e.g., coding each impact/action separately) than the binary article-level coding typically required by human labor constraints.
LLMs' multilingual capabilities allow the same coding instructions to be applied across English and German without translation, overcoming traditional language barriers in cross-lingual analysis.
Human oversight remains essential, particularly for prompt refinement and output validation, even when LLMs match or exceed human reliability.
LLMs apply learned patterns rather than truly 'understanding' content, so their use requires triangulation with human-led interpretation.
methods: Replication and extension of Feldman et al. (2015), who coded climate change coverage in four major U.S. newspapers (2006-2011).
Use of a locally deployed Llama 3.1-70b model with 6-bit quantization on high-end consumer hardware (two M3 Max processors), selected after pre-testing several 2024 state-of-the-art models.

An agentic workflow with four roles: Instructor agent (generates/refines prompts via meta-prompting), Classifier agent (codes one document at a time, resetting memory to avoid hallucination, using chain-of-thought reasoning), optional Judge agent (adjudicates conflicting codings across runs by weighing chain-of-thought rationales), and a Human Intermediary (refines prompts and validates output).

Prompting techniques including meta-prompting, task decomposition into subtasks, chain-of-thought reasoning with required direct text quotes, and pooling of multiple classifier iterations (two runs per article).

Data collected via Factiva using identical inclusion criteria ('climate change'/'global warming' in headline or lead): 3,274 U.S. articles (NYT, Washington Post, USA Today, WSJ) and 4,863 German articles (taz, Süddeutsche Zeitung, FAZ, Die Welt).
Validation via Krippendorff's alpha (target >=0.7), with an 80/20 train-validation split (513 articles for prompt refinement, 129 held out) to guard against overfitting of prompts.
German-language validation comparing LLM output to two German expert coders on 200 randomly selected articles.
findings: LLM-human reliability reached acceptable levels (Krippendorff's alpha >=0.7) for most concepts; adding the Judge agent (two classifiers plus judge) generally raised alpha values (e.g., Frame rose from 0.61 to 0.74 in English and 0.68 to 0.80 in German; Timing reached 0.81).
The 'efficacy' construct was an exception, remaining below 0.7 reliability (around 0.62-0.64) despite three prompt-refinement cycles, attributed to its theoretical vagueness and abstractness.
Reliability on the combined training+validation data was slightly higher than on the validation subset alone, indicating the final prompt remained robust and not merely overfitted.
Performance was comparable across English and German, supporting the model's multilingual coding without translation.

The LLM tended to be more sensitive than human coders, detecting coded variables more frequently (especially with the Judge agent), though this did not qualitatively change the original study's findings.
The most effective reliability improvements were reminding the model not to hallucinate, decomposing complex instructions into separate prompts, and requiring direct quotations to justify each code.
Running the full pipeline required about two weeks of continuous operation, highlighting substantial computational overhead from subtask decomposition and repeated runs.
contributions: A replicable, general agentic workflow (Instructor–Classifier–Judge–Human Intermediary) for LLM-driven content analysis that can be adapted to other coding tasks.
Practical guidelines for instructing LLMs, validating output, and handling multilingual and proprietary data within typical university computational and legal constraints.
A demonstration of local, privacy-preserving LLM deployment on consumer-grade hardware that keeps proprietary data off corporate servers.
A worked case study showing how LLMs can overcome small-sample limitations (scaling from 642 to 3,274 articles) and enable finer-grained, impact/action-level coding.
Emphasis on chain-of-thought reasoning and a transparent Judge mechanism as tools for improving replicability, transparency, and accountability over opaque human coding rationales.
framing: The paper positions itself within computational communication and media studies, specifically the methodological debate over automating content analysis. It contrasts LLMs' in-context (zero/few-shot) learning against traditional supervised machine learning (e.g., BERT-style classifiers) that require large annotated datasets, while engaging with ongoing concerns about LLM reliability, consistency, bias, and the irreplaceable role of human-led interpretation.
